text: Hey, everybody.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: My name's Eric.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'm a product manager at Traversal.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And today we're going to talk about self-driving production.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So just a quick primer on what I'll cover.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'm going to talk a little bit about how AI agents are changing the software development lifecycle.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The problems that that introduces for engineers and how AI for site reliability engineering fits in, which is where Traversal comes into play.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then I'll talk about a few examples of what this looks like in practice for enterprises that we work with at Traversal and a bit about how we built our AISRE to deliver the results that we're seeing with Fortune 500 companies.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I guess to start, some quick context on kind of the different phases of software engineering.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I'm sure you're all familiar, but at a high level, you could think about software engineering as kind of three buckets.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There's system design, like what is it that I want to build?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What's the architecture that I want to build?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There's development, which is actually writing the code, building the thing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then there's troubleshooting.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So once you build something and it's interacting with the real world, it starts to break and you need to fix it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so with the advent of coding agents, the development portion has shrunk.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Development is a lot faster.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Folks like me without any formal computer science training can now contribute production code.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so this is great.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Development's a lot faster.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Teams can do 10x more.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But then what happens to either end of the spectrum?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What happens to system design and what happens to troubleshooting?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The hope is that you spend more time on the design part thinking creatively about what it is that you want to build.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But what we actually see with the enterprises that we work with is that more and more time is being spent on troubleshooting.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Much more code is being written.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: People have less understanding of the code that's being pushed into production.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so what you end up with is more issues, more complex environments.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And instead of spending all your time on the creative architecture and design, your teams are bogged down on troubleshooting.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the data kind of bears this out.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is a big problem.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: By some accounts, enterprises are spending upwards of $400 billion a year.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: 40% of executives say that this is a problem that their teams face.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And on average, engineers are losing seven plus hours each week, just troubleshooting when they're on call.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is going to become an increasing issue that we'll all hear more about, that we'll all experience more over time, as tools like Claude Code and Codex and Cursor, which are fantastic, they are fantastic, but they result in more code and more complexity.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so what are we supposed to do about it?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There are all kinds of great observability tools, tools like Datadog, Elastic, Splunk, ServiceNow, where I worked for several years before joining Traversal.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: These are great, but there's only so much that they can do.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: These tools will tell you that something is broken.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They'll point out all the things that are broken.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They'll point out things that are maybe correlated, but they won't tell you the root cause of the issue.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And when I worked on observability products at ServiceNow, this was something I heard time and again from the customers that I served, which was like, you're telling me what's broken, you're not telling me why, and you're not telling me what to do about it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so no matter how many dashboards you create in these tools, it's not really helping teams keep up with the pace of innovation and complexity that's being added to their environments.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is not just something we believe at Traversal.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is kind of a widely held view.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Google, who kind of wrote the SRE handbook, like the Bible of site reliability engineering, has commented on this directly.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we also heard recently from Anthropic quotes where they described in their own words that LLMs are not great at this problem.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They're not great at pointing out what is the root cause of an issue.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now, why is this so hard?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What makes this so challenging?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In this particular example that we have on the screen, which was based on something we saw with one of our customers, if a checkout API is failing, you might need to make five to 10 hops across
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Like dozens of services and petabytes of data to actually get to the root cause.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so in a very small contained environment, perhaps there's a single seasoned SRE at your company that knows the full stack and can debug everything and has all the tribal knowledge to sift through all your data.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But if you're a Fortune 50 enterprise or a Fortune 100 enterprise, there's no single engineer that has all of that context.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so what you end up with is a war room with 50 engineers pulled in and many, many hours trying to debug this issue because everyone has their own particular slice of context.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: No one has kind of the full scope and breadth of this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so it's really challenging for a human or a human paired with Claude Code to get kind of the full spectrum of context needed to jump from a checkout API is failing over here, five hops away to the expired TLS certificate that maybe caused the issue.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so that's kind of what motivated our founders to launch Traversal.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Fundamentally, the belief that we have at Traversal is that root cause analysis is not an observability problem.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's a causal problem.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so that's why our four founders, three of them come from academia, one comes from QuantFinance, and they've dedicated decades of their lives towards causal machine learning, which is how do you find cause and effect, and have applied it to this problem, because it's a massive one that enterprises are really struggling with.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so that kind of brings us to the topic of this talk, which is self-driving production.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What we're building at Traversal is the ability for an enterprise to basically have a self-driving production environment.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What that means is a closed-loop system where
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: As issues break, the AI system finds the issue or the incident or the alert, finds the root cause of what caused that issue in the first place, puts up a fix, verifies that it's been fixed, and the loop is closed, hopefully without ever having to page or disrupt any of your team members so that they can keep focusing on building.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is a spectrum.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A lot of companies are not fully there yet.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We like to think of it in terms of levels, almost like self-driving cars or autonomous driving.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We think about it in the same frame.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So level zero is where most companies are today, where everything is fully manual.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You're pulling a bunch of people into a Slack war room or onto a Zoom call.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You're spending hours debugging things.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Level one might be where you have some rules and automations.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We're hearing a lot about loops that teams are building now with tools like Claude Code or Cursor or Codex.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so these might be rule-based automations where you can build out a very structured, specific workflow in response to an alert.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Those rule-based automations kind of break down when it's a novel situation.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And usually a sub one is something you haven't seen before.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There's not really a runbook for it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so the rule-based automation breaks down there.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And level two and level three is kind of where you start to get a little more automation built in.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In level three, perhaps you have like a homegrown agent that is really good at debugging issues for a specific service or a specific set of alerts.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But really where we see the leap is going from level three to level four, which is cutting across an entire environment.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So hundreds of services, like hundreds of repos, thousands of log indexes.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's quite challenging to home grow a solution that can handle that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And level five is kind of the holy grail, which is not only can we diagnose issues across a full production environment for a large enterprise, but also put up the fixes and verify the fixes as well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so we're really proud that at Traversal we get to work with and serve some of the biggest companies in the world, companies like American Express, who I spend a lot of time with personally, Pepsi, DigitalOcean, Capital One.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And it's really cool to see the volume and scale of data that Traversal is able to handle.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You know, trillions of logs that are generated, trillions of spans, tens of billions of metrics and events.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And hitting 80% plus root cause for these high severity incidents at this scale is a technical feat that we're pretty proud of.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so beyond just these kind of results at a high level,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: As a product manager, I like to think about the use cases that we build for our customers.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so there's a few different types of scenarios and use cases that we found that can deliver a lot of value.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'll dig into a few in more detail.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But at a high level, there's Alert Intelligence, a product that I spend a lot of time on, which is helping on-call teams triage and prioritize hundreds or thousands of alerts that they may be receiving in a single day, helping you deal with alert fatigue.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There is incident root cause analysis, which is where we got started.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: How do we help you find the root cause, pinpoint the root cause of an incident in minutes when it otherwise would have taken hours and dozens of engineers?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There is self-healing, which is not only telling you what the root cause was, but putting up the fix to address and mitigate that issue.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There's production support, which is the variety of questions and issues that your team might be dealing with in any given day, wanting to chat with their production environment, get specific data points that maybe aren't part of a broader incident, but are still taking up a lot of time and toil for your teams.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then pre-production, there is code resilience, like when you're putting up changes, how do you make sure that this code is making your system more resilient and reliable over time?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so at Traversal, we cover kind of the whole gamut of use cases.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But I'll dig into alert intelligence and incident root cause just to give you a bit of a more detailed sense of what that might look like, what that looks like.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I'm happy to answer any questions after about the others.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So for alert intelligence, the example that I have here is based on our engagement with Pepsi.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so Pepsi uses traversal across a bunch of their different applications, but a very core one is for their supply chain.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They have a lot of internal tooling and software to make sure that
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The raw materials and the finished product can move through their supply chain.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And a very critical piece of that is making sure that finished product gets from their warehouse to their trucks to their retailers at the end.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And before traversal, their team would get thousands or tens of thousands of alerts every single week.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And at any given time, a single engineer might have a backlog of 700 alerts.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is kind of a crippling state to be in.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Like, you have so much noise that you don't know where to look, you don't know what's broken, and things slip through the cracks.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Or you just try to keep up and burn out.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so this was a big problem that Pepsi was facing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And they use traversal to help parse the signal from the noise of these tens of thousands of alerts.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so now, instead of each engineer having a backlog of 700 alerts, they get a very prioritized and filtered set of
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Alerts that have already been pre-investigated.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We flag to them the alerts that are actually worth digging into.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We flag to them opportunities to reduce alert noise, whether that's updating the underlying alert rules in their code, dismissing alerts that don't need to be addressed right now, or creating tickets for alerts that are maybe technical debt that can be handled later on, but aren't super important to deal with at this moment.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so we've seen a lot of great results with Pepsi on this alert use case and many of our other customers as well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The next example is around incident root cause analysis.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is a case study from our engagement with Annex where I've personally spent a lot of time myself.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So before working with traversal, what an incident looked like at American Express is anywhere from five to 10 teams get paged, anywhere from 20 to 50 engineers.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And it could take, in this particular example, 60 minutes, but it could take hours or days.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: to get resolution to an incident.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can imagine if customers aren't able to pay their credit card bill, like that's a big problem.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Or if they're not able to log into their mobile app, that's a big problem.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so now Traversal is the first responder to every single incident that's created at American Express.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so what that looks like is the second the bridge is declared, that's the term they use internally, the second the incident is declared, Traversal is dispatched.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Within three minutes, we'll post a very detailed root cause analysis in the Slack channel where that incident is being managed.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We can post updates to ServiceNow tickets if they want to as well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And rather than paging five teams and 58 engineers, because you have that initial analysis, it's a lot less chaotic.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You have a sense of what actually broke.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And either no teams get paged or maybe you page the one or two teams just to verify the findings that Traversal posted.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so we save, in this case, like 50-plus engineers from the time and headache of being paged into this incident.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that's especially appreciated when these incidents are happening in the middle of the night.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Like this is a good night of sleep that 53 engineers can have now.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so those are two of the use cases that we're especially proud of at Traversal.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But like I mentioned, there's a bunch of others.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Maybe in the last couple of minutes, I'll just highlight AI site reliability engineering is a very hot space.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you're familiar, you've probably heard of a lot of companies in the space or claiming that they're solving these problems.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We think that there's a few really key questions you should be asking that are critical to getting this right.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the first is, can your AI SRE see all of your production data?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you're only giving it a slice or if it has gaps in its understanding, it's going to be very hard to get to a very detailed root cause.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The second is, can it search through this data?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's often petabytes of data, hundreds of billions of logs, without blowing up costs or taking down your observability infrastructure.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is really not trivial to do at scale for a Fortune 100 enterprise.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The third is, can it map out the relationships between all of these entities and your data?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Even if you're able to ingest and read through all this data, if you don't know what to do with it and if you're lost, it's kind of worthless.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then four, does it get better and smarter over time autonomously without having to dedicate engineering resources to maintaining a bunch of markdown files or having a bunch of forward deployed engineers taking up your team's time to maintain the system knowledge?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And finally, can it make multiple hops?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Can it find the non-trivial, non-obvious root cause that's far away from the initial symptom in a matter of minutes?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What we've seen is like anything more than five minutes and you've kind of lost the plot.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You've lost the patience of the on-call team and people will fall back onto their own habits.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So it needs to be really good.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It needs to be really fast.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I won't go into this in too much detail, but this is kind of how we think about these five questions at traversal.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So at the bottom of the stack is how we think about kind of analyzing all your data without increasing costs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So basically, how do we ingest and map all of the data that we're connected to and integrate with all of that data?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In the middle of the stack is how we make sense of that data.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so we call that our production world model.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: How do we map out all the relationships between all the data that we're ingesting?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then finally, how do we surface that and package that up in either use cases or user experiences that are valuable to your team?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so there's a lot of components to getting this right, especially at Fortune 500 scale.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so that's a bit about what we've been building at Traversal, what we're delivering at Traversal.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The core pieces, like I mentioned, are the production world model, so how we map and make sense of all the data that we integrate with, and then what we refer to as our causal search engine, basically the harness and mechanism that we give our agents to search through all of that data that we've mapped out.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so the production world model and the causal search engine are how we believe we are going to help Fortune 500 enterprises get to the level five of autonomy, fully self-driving production.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Cool.
